findings.title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is always False for spawn processes, so unhealthy flushers are never killed
findings.body: `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` creates processes of type `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which is *not* a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (that name resolves to `multiprocessing.context.Process` of the default context). Therefore the guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` never fires, and the previous unconditional `self.process.kill()` behaviour is lost. Consequence: when a flusher is declared unhealthy (hang or non-responsive), the old OS process is left running and `_create_process_for_shards()` immediately starts a second process for the *same* shards. Two processes then call `flush_segments()`/`done_flush_segments()` on the same Redis shards, which can produce duplicated segments to `buffered-segments` and leaks a process on every restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per shard group). The same wrong check is used in `join()` (line 346), so `terminate()` is also never called on shutdown. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`) instead.

findings.title: No validation of flusher_processes; negative value raises KeyError, 0 silently means one process per shard
findings.body: `--flusher-processes` is parsed as a plain int with no range validation and is used as `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` / `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`. With `--flusher-processes 0`, `0 or N` evaluates to `N`, so the operator silently gets one process per assigned shard instead of the obvious interpretation. With a negative value, `range(self.num_processes)` is empty while `i % self.num_processes` still evaluates to 0, so the shard assignment loop raises `KeyError: 0` and the consumer crashes at startup with an opaque error. Validate the option (>= 1) in the click option or in `__init__`.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag key and high-cardinality tag value for shard groups
findings.body: The produce timer and segment size metrics are tagged `{"shard": shard_tag}` (lines 185, 195) while the wait_produce timer is tagged `{"shards": shard_tag}` (line 199) — two different tag keys for the same dimension, which will silently split dashboards/queries. Worse, `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of all shards owned by the process (e.g. `"0,3,6"`), whose value depends on the Kafka partition assignment of each consumer instance and changes on every rebalance. `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` is emitted per segment, so this adds a per-assignment, unbounded-cardinality tag to a very high-volume metric. Use a single stable tag key and either omit the shard tag or emit one metric per concrete shard.

findings.title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
findings.body: Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `time.sleep` globally for the duration of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62, whose comment claims to "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", therefore returns immediately and provides no synchronisation at all. The test still races: if the flusher thread has not observed the new `current_drift` before `step.join()` sets `stopped`, `messages` stays empty and `(msg,) = messages` fails with a ValueError. Either use a real sleep (e.g. capture the original `time.sleep` before patching) or poll on `messages` with a timeout.

findings.title: New flusher test asserts a tautology and never exercises the multiprocess path
findings.body: `total_shards = sum(len(shards) for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values()); assert total_shards == 4` is trivially satisfied by the construction loop and would still pass if a shard were assigned twice while another was dropped. The meaningful invariant — that the union of `process_to_shards_map` values equals the assigned shards exactly once each — is not checked. In addition, because `produce_to_pipe` is passed, `SpanFlusher` takes the `threading.Thread` branch, so the test does not cover the actual `SpawnProcess` path this PR introduces (process creation, pickling of the per-shard `SpansBuffer`, restart/kill logic), and the factory is never shut down (`fac.shutdown()` is not called).

findings.title: Dead method _create_process_for_shard is unused and silently no-ops for unknown shards
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` has no callers anywhere after the refactor (health checking now goes through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). It is also subtly unsafe: if the shard is not found in `process_to_shards_map` it silently does nothing. Leaving it in invites a future caller to use the wrong restart path; delete it.

findings.title: Parent-side SpansBuffer per process is replaced on restart without closing the old one
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shards()` constructs a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process on every (re)start and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting the previous instance. The parent uses these buffers for `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()`, so they hold live Redis connections; the overwritten buffer is never closed, so each flusher restart leaks the old buffer's Redis client(s) in the main consumer process until GC. Note also that the `buffer` argument passed to `SpanFlusher` is now used only for `assigned_shards` — the extra parent-side buffers duplicate the Redis clients already held by the span-writing buffer.

findings.title: Docstring claims one process per shard and omits the new max_processes parameter
findings.body: The class docstring now says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the actual behaviour is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes, and the `process-spans` consumer defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, i.e. a single process handling all shards. The docstring's parameter list documents `topic` (which is not a parameter) and `produce_to_pipe`, but not the new `max_processes` argument or its `None` default (one process per shard). This will mislead operators tuning the flusher.

findings.title: join() abandons remaining processes once the deadline expires
findings.body: In `join()`, the per-process loop computes `remaining_time` only to `break` out of the whole loop when the deadline has passed. Processes later in the iteration order are then neither waited on nor terminated, so on a timed-out shutdown an arbitrary subset of flusher processes is left running (they are daemons, so they die only when the parent exits). The computed `remaining_time` is otherwise unused — the inner wait loop re-checks `deadline` instead, so the first process can consume the entire timeout. Terminate every process regardless of the deadline.
